Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Depression was more common in individuals with vitamin D deficiency; depressed subjects showed mild vitamin D deficiency while healthy subjects had sufficient levels.
Sentence: "The results of our study indicated that depression was common in individuals having vitamin D deficiency."
Measured as: depression (Beck Depression Inventory)
Population: 100 healthy and 100 depressed subjects in Peshawar, Pakistan, screened with the BDI
Intervention: Vitamin D status (measured level), no intervention given
Comparator: Healthy subjects with sufficient vitamin D
Design: case-control study
Sample size: 200
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not change mean depressive symptom scores compared with placebo in pregnant women with low vitamin D.
Sentence: "After the intervention, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups in terms of FBG (P = 0.850), FBI (P = 0.353), HOMA-IR (P = 0.632), mean score of depressive symptoms (P = 0.505), frequency of gestational diabetes (P = 0.187) and frequency of abortion (P = 1.000) and there was only a difference in terms of serum vitamin D level (P = 0.016) and musculoskeletal pain including knee pain (P = 0.025), ankle pain (P < 0.001) and leg pain (P < 0.001)."
Measured as: mean score of depressive symptoms
Population: 88 pregnant women at 8-10 weeks of pregnancy with vitamin D less than 30 ng/ml
Intervention: Vitamin D 4,000 units daily for 18 weeks
Comparator: Placebo tablets
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 88
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Responses
